```python
def knee(rows):
    """Return the concurrency where marginal gain per added stream first drops below 5 tok/s.

    rows: list of (conc, agg_tps) sorted by conc ascending.
    Returns the conc at which (delta agg_tps / delta conc) < 5, or None if never.
    """
    for (c0, t0), (c1, t1) in zip(rows, rows[1:]):
        if c1 > c0 and (t1 - t0) / (c1 - c0) < 5:
            return c1
    return None

# Example:
# rows = [(1, 40), (2, 78), (4, 150), (8, 200)]
# knee(rows) -> 8   # (200-150)/(8-4) = 12.5 ... adjust data as needed
# knee([(1, 40), (2, 78), (4, 150), (8, 160)]) -> 8  # (160-150)/4 = 2.5 < 5
```

rows.content: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by having a small, cheap "draft" model guess several tokens ahead, then letting the big model verify all of them in a single pass — if the guesses are right, you get many tokens for the price of one. Counting is nearly free to guess: after "1, 2, 3," the next token is almost certainly "4," so the draft model nails it and the big model confirms a whole run at once. Prose is the opposite: at any point there are thousands of equally plausible next words, so the draft model's guesses are usually wrong, and the big model has to reject them and fall back to generating one token at a time — meaning you pay the overhead of drafting and verifying without getting the speedup, and can even end up slower than if you'd never speculated at all.
rows.prompt: In one paragraph, explain to a smart non-engineer why a model that is fast at counting can be slow at writing prose when speculative decoding is on.

Mathematical induction is a method of proof used to establish that a statement holds for every natural number, and it is particularly well suited to claims about sums defined recursively. The claim we wish to prove is that the sum of the first n odd numbers equals n squared. In symbols, if we let S(n) denote the sum 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n − 1), then we want to show that S(n) = n² for every positive integer n. The structure of the proof has two essential parts: a base case, which verifies the statement for the smallest value of n, and an inductive step, which shows that if the statement is true for some arbitrary value k, then it must also be true for the next value k + 1. Together these two parts guarantee the statement for all natural numbers, because the base case anchors the chain and the inductive step propagates truth along it indefinitely.

For the base case, take n = 1. The sum of the first one odd number is simply 1, and n² is also 1, so the statement holds. This is a trivial verification, but it is indispensable, since without it the inductive step would prove nothing about any actual number.

# Werkbank, Licht, Geduld

Es gibt Orte, an denen die Zeit nicht vergeht, sondern sich sammelt. Glashütte ist ein solcher Ort. In diesem kleinen Tal im Osterzgebirge, wo die Müglitz sich zwischen bewaldeten Hängen hindurchwindet und im Winter der Nebel so tief hängt, dass die Kirchturmspitze darin zu verschwimmen scheint, hat sich über mehr als ein Jahrhundert eine merkwürdige Kultur herausgebildet: eine Kultur der winzigen Dinge. Wer hierherkommt, um das Handwerk des Uhrmachers zu lernen, der lernt zuerst, dass Größe nichts mit Ausdehnung zu tun hat. Ein Zahnrad von der Größe eines Stecknadelkopfes kann ein ganzes Leben füllen. Eine Unruhfeder, dünner als ein Haar, kann darüber entscheiden, ob ein Werk in fünfzig Jahren noch die richtige Stunde schlägt oder ob es verstummt ist, ein stummer Zeuge seiner selbst.

Zwischen den Halten wurde die Landschaft zu einem Fließband aus Lichtern.
